title: Every 2xx means committed
summary: A Playwright run found a bug that unit tests couldn't: the database commit ran after the response was sent. What went wrong, why it matters, and how a test now guards every route.
body:
## The symptom

In CarePulse, a Playwright end-to-end run exposed a bug that no unit test had caught: after saving a change, the page sometimes showed the old data.

The cause was ordering. The database commit was running **after the HTTP response had already been sent**. The browser received a success response, immediately fetched the record again, and could read the row before the write was committed.

## Why this is worse than it looks

A 2xx response is a promise to the client: *your change is saved*. When that promise is only true a few milliseconds later, you get failures that are:

- **Intermittent.** They depend on timing, so they pass locally and fail under load or on a slower CI runner.
- **Silent.** Nothing errors. The client simply shows stale data, and the user repeats the action or loses trust in the screen.
- **Hard to see in unit tests.** A unit test that calls a service function never sees the gap between "response sent" and "transaction committed".

In a clinic workflow the stale read is not cosmetic. A nurse who records vitals and sees the old values may enter them twice.

## The rule

The fix was to make one guarantee explicit: **every 2xx response means the write is committed.** The transaction finishes before the response leaves the server. If the commit fails, the client gets an error, not a success followed by a quiet rollback.

## Guarding it for every route

Fixing the one endpoint that failed would not stop the next endpoint from repeating the mistake. So the guarantee is enforced by a test that checks **every route**, not just the one that broke.

The general shape of such a test:

1. Enumerate the application's routes that change data.
2. Call each one through the real HTTP stack.
3. As soon as the response arrives, read the affected data through a separate database connection.
4. Fail if the change is not visible yet.

Because the test walks the whole route table, a new endpoint is covered the moment it is added.

## What I took from it

End-to-end tests earn their cost by catching problems that live *between* layers: here, between the web framework's response cycle and the database transaction. This bug was found by a test, not by reading the code.

title: Tenant isolation with PostgreSQL row-level security
summary: When several clinics share one database, one missing WHERE clause can leak another clinic's patients. Row-level security makes the database enforce the boundary as well.
body:
## The problem with filtering in code

A multi-tenant application usually keeps every tenant's rows in the same tables and filters by a tenant column. Every query needs the filter. The risk is that *one* query, written in a hurry or generated by a helper, forgets it, and one clinic's receptionist sees another clinic's patients.

CarePulse checks access in two places: a **role-permission matrix** in the application decides what a user may do, and **PostgreSQL row-level security** decides which rows the database will return at all.

## How row-level security works

Row-level security (RLS) attaches a policy to a table. Every query against that table has the policy's condition applied by PostgreSQL itself, whatever the application's SQL says.

An illustrative setup (not CarePulse's actual schema):

```sql
ALTER TABLE patients ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE patients FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON patients
  USING (clinic_id = current_setting('app.clinic_id')::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (clinic_id = current_setting('app.clinic_id')::uuid);
```

- `USING` filters the rows a query can **see**.
- `WITH CHECK` stops a query from **writing** a row into another tenant.
- `FORCE` applies the policy to the table's owner too; without it, the owner role bypasses RLS.

Each request then sets the tenant for its own transaction, so the setting can't leak into the next request on a pooled connection:

```sql
SET LOCAL app.clinic_id = '…the authenticated user''s clinic…';
```

## Things that bite

- **Superusers and roles with `BYPASSRLS` ignore policies.** The application should connect as an ordinary role.
- **A missing policy fails quietly.** A table with RLS enabled and no matching policy returns no rows rather than an error, so tests need to assert on isolation explicitly, from both sides: tenant A sees its rows, and tenant B does not.
- **Every table with tenant data needs a policy.** A new table without one is exactly the "forgot the filter" bug moved into the schema. That's a good thing to check automatically.

## Why both layers

The application layer still matters: it knows about roles, workflows and business rules that the database doesn't. RLS is the backstop. If application code gets a filter wrong, the database still refuses to return another clinic's data.

title: Background jobs that are safe to rerun
summary: A job that updates overdue follow-ups will, sooner or later, run twice at once. PostgreSQL advisory locks and idempotent updates make that harmless.
body:
## Jobs run twice

Any scheduled job will eventually overlap with itself: a deploy starts a second worker, a slow run is still going when the next one fires, or someone triggers it by hand. CarePulse has a background job that updates overdue follow-ups, and it is designed to be **safe to rerun and safe to run on several workers**.

Two properties make that true.

## 1. Only one run at a time: advisory locks

PostgreSQL advisory locks are locks on an arbitrary number that the application chooses. The database doesn't attach any meaning to them; it only guarantees that two sessions can't hold the same one at once.

An illustrative version (not CarePulse's actual code):

```python
from sqlalchemy import text

JOB_LOCK = 42_001  # any constant unique to this job

def run_overdue_followups(session):
    got_lock = session.execute(
        text("SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(:key)"), {"key": JOB_LOCK}
    ).scalar()
    if not got_lock:
        return  # another worker is already running this job

    mark_overdue_followups(session)
    session.commit()  # the transaction-level lock is released here
```

- `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock` returns immediately instead of waiting, so a second worker simply skips the run.
- The `_xact_` variant is released automatically when the transaction ends, even if the worker crashes. A session-level lock held by a crashed process would otherwise stay held until its connection closes.

## 2. Running again changes nothing: idempotent updates

A lock prevents two runs *at the same time*. It doesn't stop the job running twice *in a row*. For that, the update itself must be idempotent, which means describing the target state rather than the change:

```sql
UPDATE follow_ups
SET status = 'overdue'
WHERE status = 'scheduled'
  AND due_at < now();
```

Running this twice has the same effect as running it once: the second run finds nothing left to change.

## The combination

- The advisory lock keeps concurrent workers from stepping on each other.
- The idempotent update keeps repeated runs harmless.
- Because the lock lives in PostgreSQL, the job needs no extra infrastructure such as a separate lock service.

title: Publishing a static site from an admin, through Git
summary: This portfolio is fully static, yet it has an admin panel. Edits become commits on a draft branch, and publishing is one commit laid over the current main branch.
body:
## The constraint

This site is pre-rendered: every public page is static HTML built by Next.js. That's fast and cheap to host, but it means there is no database to edit. The content lives in JSON files in the repository, validated at build time so that a malformed edit fails the build instead of reaching the live site.

The admin panel had to fit that model rather than replace it.

## Drafts are a branch

When content is saved in the admin, it isn't written to the live branch. It becomes a commit on a separate `admin-draft` branch, created from `main` the first time something is saved. Drafts therefore survive closed tabs and different devices, and each save is inspectable in Git like any other commit.

## Publishing is one commit

Publishing takes the files the draft changed and lays them over the **current** `main` in a single new commit. It doesn't merge the draft branch, because code may have been pushed to `main` since the draft started and a naive "replace everything with the draft" would revert it.

The update is made with `force: false`, so GitHub refuses it if `main` moved between reading it and writing the new commit. Vercel then deploys the commit like any other push.

## Rollback is a new commit, too

Rolling back a published change never rewrites history. It creates a new commit that restores the content files a previous commit changed, and leaves code files alone. The history always says what happened.

## What the admin can't touch

The GitHub token the admin uses can write only to the content folder and the managed public folders (logos, screenshots, portrait, résumés). A request for any other path is refused before it reaches GitHub, so a bug in the admin can't modify the site's code.

## Why this design

- **No database to run**, and the public site stays fully static.
- **History and rollback for free**, because every change is a commit.
- **The build is the final check.** The same validators run in the admin form, in the server action and in `next build`.
